title: Minecraft's toughest challenge just fell to an AI tag team that costs pennies to run
excerpt: A tiny token bill funded a lightning fast collaboration where Astra worked as the planner and Jev as the executer of those plans.
content_html:
Published Sep 21, 2026, 9:44 AM EDT

Hamed holds a B.A. in English Literature, graduating cum laude. He loves music, tech gadgets, and exploring the latest in the world of LLMs. He also enjoys tinkering with creative software such as Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Photoshop.

A lifelong musician, Hamed plays multiple instruments, including guitar, bass, and oud. He is equally fascinated by smart-home technology and can happily spend hours geeking out over connected lights, speakers, sensors, and automations that make everyday life a little more interesting. When he isn’t covering the latest tech news, he explores more creative topics on his Medium blog, works on his music, or clears his head by riding his motorcycle.

Summary

  • Jev + Astra beat Minecraft’s Ender Dragon in 8m43s for under $1.
  • Astra planned; Jev made fast, structured choices to execute tight in‑game actions.
  • Combining System 1 (Jev) and System 2 (Astra) models yields faster, cheaper agents.

A tester on X (Twitter) recently paired Jev with Astra to defeat Minecraft’s Ender Dragon in just 8 minutes and 43 seconds. What's more impressive is that the whole operation cost less than a dollar in tokens.

By comparison, Vals AI livestreamed a separate Minecraft run powered by Astra for 141 hours. That experiment never finished the game, and the model eventually spent much of its time farming potatoes instead of progressing toward the Ender Dragon.

Astra was the brains, and Jev was the muslce

Jev changed how the agent made decisions

Last week, the story of GPT Astra’s 141-hour Minecraft run became popular on X. After a Creeper blew up Astra's in-game chest and bed, the AI model seemed very frustrated and demotivated to continue the game, appearing to be reflecting on its loss on a rainy day and refusing to do much besides farming potatoes.

While X users gave the experiment a cute narrative, we explored the more serious lessons its behavior offered about autonomous AI agents facing unexpected situations. One was the need for controlled environments and recovery plans when running autonomous agents. Such safeguards are important not only because LLMs can make serious mistakes, but also because an AI agent can get stuck in an unproductive loop and continue consuming tokens without achieving anything useful.

Now, the same GPT Astra managed to finish the run and kill the Ender Dragon in under 9 minutes, thanks to getting help from Jev: a recently developed AI model that operates vastly differently from what we've seen with OpenAI or Anthropic models.

Ronak Malde, the tester behind this Minecraft run, explained how the combo worked. Astra acted as the planner and set objectives, item targets, and travel waypoints. Receiving instructions from Astra, Jev would then make decisions about operating the character in game via access to WASD, space, click, and mouse movements. Ronak made the full code available on GitHub.

How Jev helped Astra achieve what it couldn't achieve alone

Large language models like Astra are designed to understand instructions and generate natural-sounding responses. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex apply generative models to software-development tasks. While these state-of-the-art systems are impressive, they are not designed primarily to make large numbers of fast, tightly constrained decisions that software can use directly. That is the job Jev was built to perform.

Instead of generating text or code, Jev receives unstructured information about a program's current state, alongside predefined questions. Then, it chooses from the possible answers you provide. It can select one option from a list, assign a score, or estimate the probability of a yes-or-no outcome. This makes it useful for quick, repetitive tasks such as deciding what an AI agent should do next.

Developed by TypeSafe AI, a company founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida, Jev operates differently from conventional text-based LLMs. The company calls it a “System One” model, a term borrowed from psychologist Daniel Kahneman's distinction between two forms of thinking in humans. "System 1" describes fast and automatic judgment calls, whereas "System 2" refers to slower, more deliberate reasoning for complex and abstract problems.

Jev reflects the first category by returning structured decisions quickly instead of generating free-form text. Advanced models like Astra, on the other hand, sit closer to the System 2 side of the analogy, since they can work through open-ended problems using advanced reasoning. The problem is that these System 2 models require a lot more time and computing power. For tasks like automations and decision-making with a limited, pre-defined set of options, Jev can be dramatically more time- and recourse-efficient.

If there's one thing we can deduce from this impressive AI tag-team is this: the future of capable AI agents may depend less on building one superb model that tackles everything, and more on giving each model the job it does best for better performance.
